summary_notes.overview: A matrix is simply a neat, rectangular grid of numbers or functions arranged in rows and columns. It helps us organize data, like tracking how many notebooks and pens different people have, in a structured way.

core_concepts.title: What is a Matrix?
core_concepts.detail: A matrix is an ordered rectangular array of numbers or functions. Think of it as a table where the data is neatly lined up in rows (horizontal) and columns (vertical).

core_concepts.title: Elements (Entries)
core_concepts.detail: The individual numbers or functions inside the matrix are called elements or entries. For example, in the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 15 & 6 \\ 10 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, the numbers $15, 6, 10,$ and $2$ are the elements.

core_concepts.title: Rows and Columns
core_concepts.detail: Rows are the horizontal lines of elements, and columns are the vertical lines of elements. The size of a matrix is described by the number of rows followed by the number of columns (e.g., a $2 \times 3$ matrix has 2 rows and 3 columns).

core_concepts.title: Notation
core_concepts.detail: Matrices are usually denoted by capital letters like $A, B, C$. The elements are often written with square brackets $[\ ]$ or parentheses $(\ )$.

key_definitions.definition: An ordered rectangular array of numbers or functions.
Each individual number or function in a matrix.
A horizontal line of elements in a matrix.
A vertical line of elements in a matrix.

high_yield_takeaways: A matrix is just a structured table of numbers or functions.
The order of elements matters, so it is called an 'ordered' array.
Matrices can contain numbers, variables, or even functions like $\sin x$ or $\cos x$.
The size of a matrix is always written as (rows) $\times$ (columns).
Square brackets $[\ ]$ are the most common way to write matrices.

governing_formulas.name: Matrix Size Notation
governing_formulas.note: $m$ is the number of rows, and $n$ is the number of columns.

governing_formulas.name: General Matrix Form
governing_formulas.note: $a_{ij}$ represents the element in the $i$-th row and $j$-th column.

exam_traps.trap: Confusing rows and columns when stating the size of a matrix.
exam_traps.remedy: Always remember: Size = (Rows) $\times$ (Columns). Count the horizontal lines first, then the vertical lines.

exam_traps.trap: Thinking matrices can only contain numbers.
exam_traps.remedy: Matrices can also contain variables, functions, or even other matrices. Just keep the rectangular shape!

quick_quiz.question: What is a matrix?

options.text: A random list of numbers
An ordered rectangular array of numbers or functions
A single number in brackets
A graph of a function

quick_quiz.explanation: A matrix is specifically an ordered rectangular array of numbers or functions. The order and rectangular shape are key.

quick_quiz.question: In a matrix, what are the horizontal lines of elements called?

options.text: Columns
Rows
Entries
Elements

quick_quiz.explanation: Horizontal lines of elements are called rows. Vertical lines are called columns.

quick_quiz.question: If a matrix has 3 rows and 2 columns, what is its size?

options.text: $2 \times 3$
$3 \times 2$
$5 \times 1$
$1 \times 5$

quick_quiz.explanation: The size of a matrix is always written as (number of rows) $\times$ (number of columns). So, 3 rows and 2 columns means $3 \times 2$.

quick_quiz.question: What are the individual numbers or functions inside a matrix called?

options.text: Rows
Columns
Elements or Entries
Arrays

quick_quiz.explanation: The individual numbers or functions in a matrix are called elements or entries.

summary_notes.overview: A relation between two sets $A$ and $B$ is any collection of ordered pairs from $A\times B$. A function is a special relation where each element of $A$ appears exactly once as the first entry.

core_concepts.title: Relation
core_concepts.detail: A relation $R$ from $A$ to $B$ is a subset $R\subseteq A\times B$. If $(a,b)\in R$, we write $a\,R\,b$.

core_concepts.title: Function
core_concepts.detail: A function $f\colon A\to B$ is a relation where every $a\in A$ is paired with exactly one $b\in B$.

core_concepts.title: Domain, Codomain, Range
core_concepts.detail: Domain is the set of all first elements, codomain is the set $B$ we map into, and range (image) is the set of all second elements actually used.

key_definitions.definition: $A\times B$ is the set of all ordered pairs $(a,b)$ with $a\in A$ and $b\in B$.
An ordered pair $(a,b)$ keeps the order; $(a,b)\neq(b,a)$ unless $a=b$.
A function that has a reverse mapping $f^{-1}$, possible only when each $b$ in the range comes from exactly one $a$.

high_yield_takeaways: A relation is just any set of ordered pairs from $A\times B$.
Every function is a relation, but not every relation is a function.
For a function, each element of the domain appears once on the left side.

governing_formulas.name: Relation definition
governing_formulas.note: $R$ contains the pairs that satisfy the given rule.

governing_formulas.name: Function definition
governing_formulas.latex: $f\colon A\to B\;\text{with}\;\forall a\in A,\;\exists!\,b\in B:\;(a,b)\in f$

exam_traps.trap: Mixing up relation and function.
exam_traps.remedy: Check if every element of the domain has exactly one partner; if not, it’s only a relation.

exam_traps.trap: Ignoring the order of the pair.
exam_traps.remedy: Remember $(a,b)$ is different from $(b,a)$; always write the first element from the domain set.

quick_quiz.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes a function?

options.text: Each element of the domain is paired with exactly one element of the codomain.
A function can pair one domain element with many codomain elements.
A function is any subset of $A\times B$.
The order of elements in a pair does not matter for a function.

quick_quiz.explanation: A function must assign one and only one output to each input; options B, C, D describe relations or incorrect ideas.

quick_quiz.question: If $R\subseteq A\times B$ contains the pair $(a,b)$, what can we say?

options.text: $a$ is related to $b$ under $R$.
$b$ is related to $a$ under $R$.
Both $a$ and $b$ belong to the same set.
The pair $(b,a)$ must also be in $R$.

quick_quiz.explanation: By definition, $(a,b)\in R$ means $a\,R\,b$. The relation does not automatically include $(b,a)$.

topic_study_top_chap_book_c12_phy_2026_1.topic_title: Fundamentals of Electric Charge & Coulomb's Law

summary_notes.overview: Electric charge is a tiny, quantised property of particles that can be positive or negative. Like charges push each other away, while opposite charges pull together.

core_concepts.title: Electric Charge
core_concepts.detail: Charge is a scalar quantity that can be positive (protons) or negative (electrons). It is always a multiple of the elementary charge $e = 1.602	imes10^{-19},	ext{C}$, written as $q = ne$ where $n$ is an integer.

core_concepts.title: Coulomb’s Law
core_concepts.detail: The force between two point charges is proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: $F = k,dfrac{|q_1q_2|}{r^2}$, where $k = 8.99	imes10^9,	ext{N m}^2	ext{/C}^2$.

key_definitions.definition: The smallest unit of electric charge, carried by an electron or a proton.
Two charges of the same sign that repel each other.
Two charges of opposite sign that attract each other.
Charge can only exist in whole multiples of the elementary charge.
The total charge in an isolated system never changes.

high_yield_takeaways: Charge is always an integer multiple of $e$.
Like charges repel, unlike charges attract.
Charge is conserved in any closed system.

governing_formulas.name: Charge quantisation
governing_formulas.note: $n$ is an integer, $e$ is the elementary charge.

exam_traps.trap: Mixing up the sign of charge with its magnitude
exam_traps.remedy: Always write the sign separately from the magnitude, e.g., $q = +3e$ or $q = -2e$.

exam_traps.trap: Forgetting the $r^2$ term in Coulomb’s law
exam_traps.remedy: Remember the force falls off with the square of the distance.

quick_quiz.question: Which of the following is true about electric charge?

options.text: Like charges attract each other.
Unlike charges repel each other.
Charge is a vector quantity.
Charge is always conserved in an isolated system.

quick_quiz.explanation: Charge is a scalar that is conserved in any closed system, so option D is correct.

summary_notes.overview: Solids are rigid materials where particles are tightly packed in a fixed arrangement. They are classified based on how these particles are arranged, either in a regular pattern (crystalline) or a random one (amorphous).

core_concepts.title: Rigidity and Density
core_concepts.detail: In solids, particles are held together by strong forces, making them rigid and dense. They have a definite shape and volume.

core_concepts.title: Crystalline Solids
core_concepts.detail: These solids have particles arranged in a highly ordered, repeating 3D pattern. They have a sharp melting point and are anisotropic (properties vary by direction).

core_concepts.title: Amorphous Solids
core_concepts.detail: These solids have a short-range order but a random arrangement overall. They have a gradual melting range and are isotropic (properties are the same in all directions).

key_definitions.definition: A property that has the same value in all directions (e.g., refractive index in glass).
A property that has different values in different directions (e.g., electrical conductivity in graphite).
The smallest repeating unit of a crystal lattice that shows the full symmetry of the crystal structure.

high_yield_takeaways: Solids have a definite shape and volume because their particles are closely packed.
Crystalline solids have a sharp melting point, while amorphous solids soften over a range of temperatures.
Crystalline solids are anisotropic; amorphous solids are isotropic.
Examples of amorphous solids include glass, rubber, and plastics.
Examples of crystalline solids include NaCl, diamond, and quartz.

governing_formulas.name: Density of a Unit Cell
governing_formulas.note: $Z$ is the number of atoms per unit cell, $M$ is molar mass, $N_A$ is Avogadro's number, and $a$ is the edge length.

exam_traps.trap: Confusing amorphous solids with liquids because they lack long-range order.
exam_traps.remedy: Remember that amorphous solids are rigid and have a definite shape, unlike liquids which flow.

exam_traps.trap: Thinking all solids have a sharp melting point.
exam_traps.remedy: Only crystalline solids have a sharp melting point. Amorphous solids melt over a range.

quick_quiz.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of amorphous solids?

options.text: Sharp melting point
Long-range order
Isotropic nature
Anisotropic nature

quick_quiz.explanation: Amorphous solids have a random arrangement of particles, making their properties the same in all directions (isotropic). Crystalline solids are anisotropic.

quick_quiz.question: Why do crystalline solids have a sharp melting point?

options.text: They have weak intermolecular forces.
They have a regular, repeating arrangement of particles.
They are isotropic.
They have a low density.

quick_quiz.explanation: The regular, repeating arrangement means all particles are held with similar strength, so they all break free at the same temperature, leading to a sharp melting point.

quick_quiz.question: Which of the following is an example of a crystalline solid?

options.text: Glass
Rubber
Quartz
Plastic

quick_quiz.explanation: Quartz is a crystalline solid with a regular arrangement of silica tetrahedra. Glass, rubber, and plastic are amorphous solids.

summary_notes.overview: Solutions are mixtures where a solute is uniformly spread in a solvent. They are described by how much solute is present per amount of solvent or solution.

core_concepts.title: Types of solutions
core_concepts.detail: Solutions can be solid, liquid or gaseous, and the solute may be a solid, liquid or gas.

core_concepts.title: Expressing concentration
core_concepts.detail: Concentration tells how much solute is present. Common ways are mass percent, molarity ($M = \frac{n}{V}$), and mole fraction ($X_{solute}=\frac{n_{solute}}{n_{total}}$).

key_definitions.definition: The substance that is dissolved in a solution.
The substance that does the dissolving; it is present in larger amount.
Number of moles of solute per litre of solution.
Mass of solute divided by total mass of solution, multiplied by 100.

high_yield_takeaways: Molarity uses volume of the whole solution, not just the solvent.
Mass percent is useful when dealing with solid mixtures.

exam_traps.trap: Using solvent volume instead of solution volume for molarity.
exam_traps.remedy: Always remember $V$ is the total volume after the solute is added.

exam_traps.trap: Confusing mass percent with percent by volume.
exam_traps.remedy: Check the units: mass percent uses grams, volume percent uses millilitres or litres.

quick_quiz.question: What is the correct expression for molarity of a solution?

options.text: $M = \frac{n_{solute}}{V_{solution}}$
$M = \frac{m_{solute}}{V_{solvent}}$
$M = \frac{n_{solute}}{m_{solution}}$
$M = \frac{m_{solute}}{m_{solvent}}$

quick_quiz.explanation: Molarity is defined as moles of solute per litre of the whole solution.

summary_notes.overview: Ideal solutions follow Raoult's law exactly, while non‑ideal solutions deviate due to molecular interactions. Colligative properties such as boiling‑point elevation help determine the molar mass of a solute.

core_concepts.title: Ideal Solution
core_concepts.detail: In an ideal solution the vapor pressure of each component is proportional to its mole fraction: $P_i = X_i P_i^{\text{pure}}$.

core_concepts.title: Non‑ideal Solution
core_concepts.detail: Real solutions show positive or negative deviation from Raoult's law because of stronger or weaker intermolecular forces.

core_concepts.title: Colligative Property – Boiling‑Point Elevation
core_concepts.detail: The rise in boiling point is given by $\Delta T_b = K_b \cdot m$, where $m = \frac{n_{solute}}{\text{mass of solvent (kg)}}$.

core_concepts.title: Molar Mass Determination
core_concepts.detail: Re‑arranging the boiling‑point formula gives $M = \frac{K_b \cdot w_{solvent} \cdot 1000}{\Delta T_b \cdot \text{mass of solute}}$.

key_definitions.definition: The vapor pressure of a component in an ideal solution equals its mole fraction times its pure‑component vapor pressure.
The ratio of moles of component $i$ to total moles in the mixture.
A property that depends only on the number of solute particles, not on their identity.

high_yield_takeaways: Ideal solutions obey $P_i = X_i P_i^{\text{pure}}$; deviations signal non‑ideality.
Boiling‑point elevation uses $\Delta T_b = K_b \cdot m$ to find molar mass.

governing_formulas.name: Raoult's Law
governing_formulas.note: $P_i$ = vapor pressure of component i, $X_i$ = mole fraction, $P_i^{\text{pure}}$ = vapor pressure of pure i

governing_formulas.name: Molar Mass from Boiling‑Point Elevation
governing_formulas.note: $w_{solvent}$ = mass of solvent (g), $m_{solute}$ = mass of solute (g)

exam_traps.trap: Using mass of solution instead of mass of solvent in $m$
exam_traps.remedy: Always use the mass of the pure solvent when calculating molality.

exam_traps.trap: Confusing mole fraction with mass fraction
exam_traps.remedy: Convert masses to moles first, then compute $X_i = \frac{n_i}{\sum n}$.

quick_quiz.question: Which expression correctly represents Raoult's law for component A in an ideal solution?

options.text: $P_A = X_A \; P_A^{\text{pure}}$
$P_A = K_b \; m$
$\Delta T_b = K_b \; X_A$
$M = \frac{K_b \; w_{solvent}}{\Delta T_b}$

quick_quiz.explanation: Raoult's law states that the vapor pressure of a component equals its mole fraction times its pure‑component vapor pressure.

summary_notes.overview: Surface chemistry is the study of what happens at the boundary where two different phases meet, like a liquid and a gas. It is crucial because many important reactions and processes occur right at these surfaces.

core_concepts.title: Phases and Interfaces
core_concepts.detail: A phase is a physically distinct part of a system (like solid, liquid, or gas). The interface is the boundary layer where two phases meet, such as the surface of water in air.

core_concepts.title: Heterogeneous vs. Homogeneous
core_concepts.detail: Surface chemistry deals with heterogeneous systems, where the composition is not uniform throughout. This is different from homogeneous systems like a pure liquid.

core_concepts.title: Surface Energy
core_concepts.detail: Molecules at the surface have higher energy than those inside the bulk because they are not surrounded by similar molecules on all sides. This leads to phenomena like surface tension.

key_definitions.definition: The branch of chemistry that studies the behavior of substances at the interface between two phases.
The boundary region where two different phases (e.g., solid-liquid, liquid-gas) come into contact.

high_yield_takeaways: Surface chemistry focuses on the **interface** between two phases.
It is a branch of **physical chemistry** dealing with heterogeneous systems.
Key phenomena include adsorption, catalysis, and colloids.
Molecules at the surface have unbalanced forces, leading to higher potential energy.

governing_formulas.name: Surface Tension (Conceptual)
governing_formulas.note: $\gamma$ is surface tension, $F$ is force, and $L$ is length. It represents the energy required to increase the surface area.

exam_traps.trap: Confusing surface chemistry with general solution chemistry.
exam_traps.remedy: Remember: Surface chemistry is specifically about the **boundary** (interface), not the bulk of the solution.

exam_traps.trap: Thinking all chemical reactions happen in the bulk.
exam_traps.remedy: Many important reactions (like catalysis) happen specifically **at the surface** of a solid.

quick_quiz.question: What is the primary focus of surface chemistry?

options.text: The behavior of molecules in the bulk of a liquid
The behavior of substances at the interface between two phases
The study of pure gases only
The internal structure of solid crystals

quick_quiz.explanation: Surface chemistry specifically studies what happens at the boundary (interface) where two different phases, like liquid and gas, meet.

quick_quiz.question: Why do molecules at the surface of a liquid have higher energy than those in the bulk?

options.text: They are moving faster due to heat
They experience unbalanced intermolecular forces
They are lighter than bulk molecules
They are repelled by the container walls

quick_quiz.explanation: Bulk molecules are pulled equally in all directions by neighbors. Surface molecules are pulled inward and sideways but not outward, creating an imbalance and higher potential energy.

summary_notes.overview: Catalysis is the process where a substance called a catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up. Catalysts can be solids, liquids, or gases, and they work by lowering the energy barrier needed for the reaction to happen.

core_concepts.title: What is a Catalyst?
core_concepts.detail: A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction but remains chemically unchanged at the end. It is not consumed in the reaction.

core_concepts.title: How Catalysts Work
core_concepts.detail: Catalysts provide an alternative pathway for the reaction with a lower activation energy ($E_a$). This means more reactant particles have enough energy to react, speeding up the process.

core_concepts.title: Types of Catalysts
core_concepts.detail: Catalysts are classified based on their physical state relative to the reactants. Homogeneous catalysts are in the same phase (e.g., liquid), while heterogeneous catalysts are in a different phase (e.g., solid catalyst with gas reactants).

core_concepts.title: Enzymes as Biological Catalysts
core_concepts.detail: Enzymes are biological catalysts found in living organisms. They are highly specific, meaning each enzyme usually catalyzes only one specific reaction (e.g., Urease breaks down urea).

key_definitions.definition: The process of increasing the rate of a chemical reaction by adding a catalyst.
The minimum energy required for reactants to transform into products. Catalysts lower this energy requirement.
Catalysis where the catalyst and reactants are in the same physical state (e.g., all liquids or all gases).
Catalysis where the catalyst and reactants are in different physical states (e.g., solid catalyst with gas reactants).

high_yield_takeaways: A catalyst is not consumed in the reaction; it is regenerated at the end.
Catalysts lower the activation energy ($E_a$), not the enthalpy change ($\Delta H$) of the reaction.
Heterogeneous catalysts often work by adsorption, where reactants stick to the catalyst surface.
Enzymes are highly specific and work best at specific temperatures and pH levels.
Common industrial catalysts include Iron ($Fe$) for ammonia synthesis and Platinum ($Pt$) for catalytic converters.

governing_formulas.name: Arrhenius Equation (Conceptual)
governing_formulas.note: Shows that lowering activation energy ($E_a$) increases the rate constant ($k$), thus speeding up the reaction.

exam_traps.trap: Thinking the catalyst changes the equilibrium position.
exam_traps.remedy: Remember: Catalysts speed up both forward and reverse reactions equally. They help reach equilibrium faster but do not change the final equilibrium constant ($K_{eq}$).

exam_traps.trap: Confusing homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts.
exam_traps.remedy: Check the physical states. If the catalyst is a solid and reactants are gases/liquids, it's heterogeneous. If all are in the same phase (e.g., liquid), it's homogeneous.

exam_traps.trap: Assuming enzymes are consumed.
exam_traps.remedy: Enzymes are biological catalysts. Like all catalysts, they are not used up; they are released unchanged after the reaction.

quick_quiz.question: What is the primary effect of a catalyst on a chemical reaction?

options.text: It increases the activation energy ($E_a$).
It lowers the activation energy ($E_a$).
It changes the enthalpy change ($\Delta H$) of the reaction.
It shifts the equilibrium constant ($K_{eq}$) to the right.

quick_quiz.explanation: Catalysts work by providing a new reaction pathway with a lower activation energy ($E_a$). This allows more particles to react successfully, speeding up the reaction. They do not change $\Delta H$ or $K_{eq}$.

quick_quiz.question: In the Haber process for ammonia synthesis, Iron ($Fe$) is used as a catalyst. What type of catalysis is this?

options.text: Homogeneous, because $Fe$ is a metal.
Heterogeneous, because $Fe$ is a solid and reactants are gases.
Autocatalysis, because the product acts as a catalyst.
Negative catalysis, because it slows down the reaction.

quick_quiz.explanation: In the Haber process, Nitrogen ($N_2$) and Hydrogen ($H_2$) are gases, while Iron ($Fe$) is a solid. Since the catalyst and reactants are in different phases, it is heterogeneous catalysis.

quick_quiz.question: Which of the following is an example of a biological catalyst?

options.text: Platinum ($Pt$)
Sulfuric Acid ($H_2SO_4$)
Urease
Nickel ($Ni$)

quick_quiz.explanation: Urease is an enzyme found in living organisms that catalyzes the breakdown of urea. Enzymes are biological catalysts. Platinum, Sulfuric Acid, and Nickel are inorganic catalysts.

quick_quiz.question: What happens to the equilibrium position of a reaction when a catalyst is added?

options.text: It shifts to the right, producing more products.
It shifts to the left, producing more reactants.
It remains unchanged, but equilibrium is reached faster.
It depends on the temperature of the reaction.

quick_quiz.explanation: A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally. Therefore, it does not change the equilibrium position or the equilibrium constant ($K_{eq}$); it only helps the system reach equilibrium more quickly.
